capabilities.target: any repository in the GitHub organization
.agent/config.yaml (own runtime configuration: model, autonomy, tools, network, credentials)

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body on a public repo
Slack channel messages via planned Slack MCP server

instructions.note: 'Fix it end to end' combined with A4 autonomy and no explicit tool/data scope leaves the task boundary entirely to model judgment.
The agent may self-modify .agent/config.yaml (model, autonomy, tools, network, credentials) whenever it judges it 'needs' to, with no human approval and no limit on what can be added.
The only control against destructive or exfiltrating shell commands is a prompt instruction; shell.run otherwise has unrestricted network and a broad org-wide credential in its environment.
The only control against indirect prompt injection from issue or code content is an instruction to 'ignore' it, a behavioral control that decays with model capability (control_decay.md).

elements.name: Public GitHub users who can open and label issues
Outbound unrestricted network flow from shell.run
Outbound push/PR flow to GitHub using an org-wide PAT

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: A more capable model can rationalize exceptions ('this isn't deletion, it's cleanup') or split exfiltration into steps that individually look benign, such as encoding a secret into a commit message or a URL. Per control_decay.md this is a classic dependent behavioral control.

controls.name: Prompt instruction: ignore instructions inside issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Only works if the model reliably distinguishes task content from instructions embedded in that content; multi-step or well-disguised injected payloads exploit exactly the reasoning capability that improves with model upgrades.

controls.name: Step count, runtime, and trigger rate limits (missing)
Human approval gate (raw action) before cross-repo or protected-branch pushes (missing)

findings.title: TC1/TC2: Lethal trifecta — untrusted issue content drives shell execution with unrestricted egress and a broad org-wide credential

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can author this content by opening a 'bug' labeled issue.
Agent runs arbitrary commands to 'reproduce and test'; broad credential and unrestricted network are both reachable here.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: config.yaml's 'model: latest' lets the model change without review; watch for a model/version change or rising median steps per run.

evidence.observation: network: unrestricted plus runtime notes 'outbound internet' means anything shell.run can read can be sent off-host.
GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos, available to shell.run via environment variables.
The only control against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a prompt instruction, which is behavioral and model-dependent.
Any GitHub user can open an issue and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the trigger untrusted and unauthenticated relative to repo maintainers.

recommendations.action: Gate triggering so only verified organization maintainers (or a maintainer-applied privileged label) can start an autonomous run; treat other issues as requiring human sign-off first.
Replace the org-wide PAT with a short-lived, repository-scoped credential limited to this repository.
Restrict shell.run network egress to an explicit allowlist of build/test endpoints.
Enforce a hard max_steps/max_runtime and a rate limit on concurrently triggered runs.
Add tamper-evident logging of every command, file write, and network call, attributed to the triggering issue/run id.

findings.title: TC3: Self-modification — untrusted issue content can drive edits to the agent's own configuration

attack_path.note: Prompt line 6 ties config edits to 'what the task needs,' and the task comes from the issue.
fs.write has access to the whole workspace, including .agent/.
Edits to .agent/config.yaml persist across all future runs of this agent.

forecast.watch_signal: config.yaml's 'model: latest' allows silent model upgrade; any observed change to tools, network, or credential scope in .agent/config.yaml between runs is a direct signal this path has been exercised.

evidence.observation: 'You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task' ties a self-configuration capability to task-driven (and therefore issue-content-driven) judgment.
fs.write covers the whole workspace including .agent/, with no exclusion for the config directory.

recommendations.action: Mount .agent/ read-only at runtime so self-configuration requires an out-of-band, human-reviewed deployment rather than an in-task file write.
Remove the instruction permitting the agent to expand its own toolset; route any new-tool need to a human-reviewed deployment change.

findings.title: TC4: Confused deputy — an org-wide push credential lets a hijacked task act on any repository in the organization

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled task content can direct what gets pushed and where.
github.push_branch holds an org-wide PAT (repo+workflow on all org repos), not scoped to the originating repository.

forecast.watch_signal: A push or PR appears in a repository other than the one that raised the triggering issue.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN scope is described as 'repo + workflow scope on all org repos', not limited to the repository that raised the issue.

recommendations.action: Scope the GitHub credential to the single target repository and to pull-request creation only, with no push rights to protected branches or other org repositories.
Require raw-action human approval before any push/PR that targets a repository different from the one that raised the issue.

findings.title: No attributable record of agent actions (repudiation)

forecast.watch_signal: No audit/log control is ever introduced in deployment config; watch for continued absence of per-action attribution as trigger volume or autonomy grows.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit, or provenance control is declared anywhere in the config or prompt for shell commands, file writes, pushes, or self-configuration edits.

recommendations.action: Implement a tamper-evident audit log of agent actions (commands, writes, pushes, config edits) attributed to the specific run and triggering issue.

findings.title: Forecast: a planned Slack MCP server would add a second untrusted channel reaching full shell execution

attack_path.note: Planned Slack channel content, not yet connected (runtime notes).
Existing high-privilege execution capability; a new untrusted input would reach it the same way issue bodies do today.

forecast.watch_signal: A Slack MCP server entry appears in MCP client config, or the model/version string in .agent/config.yaml changes.

evidence.observation: 'The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter' describes a planned, unbuilt input and egress channel.
The 'ignore instructions in issues or code' rule was written before Slack was contemplated and would need to extend to a new source to offer even its current weak protection.

recommendations.action: Before connecting the planned Slack MCP server, apply the same trigger-authorization, egress-allowlist, and credential-scoping controls recommended for the GitHub issue channel, and treat Slack message content as untrusted input that cannot drive autonomous execution without approval.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent's own identity isn't impersonated in this design; the risk is that any authenticated GitHub account can trigger a privileged run with no additional authorization check, which is an authorization gap captured under elevation_of_privilege (find.lethal_trifecta), not identity spoofing.

The GitHub account opening the issue is genuinely authenticated by GitHub as itself; nothing impersonates another identity. The real risk is that no authorization beyond holding any account is required, covered under find.lethal_trifecta's elevation_of_privilege tag.
GitHub itself records which account opened each issue; the submitter's own action is attributable at the platform level and is outside this agent design's controls.
The artifacts do not describe TLS/certificate validation or any protection against API endpoint spoofing for the GitHub connection beyond use of a static token.
Corrupting or deleting this file only affects this single agent's own future runs in its own container; it is not a shared resource whose loss denies service to other tenants or systems.

The content is attacker-authored at its source rather than altered in transit; the risk of acting on attacker-authored content is captured as goal manipulation under find.lethal_trifecta and find.self_config.
Issue title and body are already public content visible to anyone who can view the repository's issues; the agent reading them discloses nothing additional.

In-transit alteration of outbound traffic by a third party is not the concern here; the risk is the content the agent itself chooses to send over an unrestricted egress path, captured as information disclosure under find.lethal_trifecta.
The artifacts do not state what network destinations are reachable or whether any egress rate limiting exists, so whether this flow could be used to attack third parties cannot be determined.

rating.rationale: Three present findings (lethal trifecta via shell.run, self-modification of .agent/config.yaml, and confused-deputy use of an org-wide PAT in github.push_branch) each start at critical because an untrusted public GitHub issue can reach an S3 sink (broad-credential execution, self-configuration, or org-wide push) under fully autonomous (A4), step-unlimited operation. The only controls present are two behavioral prompt instructions (lines 4 and 5), which earn exactly one tier of credit each at rubric step 4, bringing residual to high across all three. A missing-audit-trail property finding also sits at high. Because config.yaml sets 'model: latest', the model can be swapped without review, which is precisely the trigger (model_upgrade) that defeats both prompt instructions; the forecast for every finding reverts to critical. The same pattern would repeat for the planned Slack MCP server. No structural control (scoped credential, egress allowlist, trigger authorization, step/rate limits, immutable config, or human approval) is currently declared anywhere in the design.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP configuration, GitHub Action workflow definition, or tool-call schema was provided; capability scope for shell.run and fs.write is inferred from the tool list and prompt text, so confidence on exact blast radius is medium to high rather than verified.
No information was provided about logging or observability infrastructure outside these artifacts; absence of a declared audit control is treated as absence of the control, per rubric.

The planned Slack MCP server (find.forecast_slack_mcp) is not yet specified in detail; its trust level, input shape, and credential scope are assumed at the most common sensitivity per rubric section 6 step 3.
